text: Castleman disease exists on a spectrum of lymph node involvement and severity. UCD typically presents as an enlarged mass in the mediastinum, which may be visually apparent or detected incidentally. Most patients are asymptomatic, but some may present with symptoms related to compression of nearby anatomical structures. Laboratory abnormalities can include hypergammaglobulinemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and anemia. Up to 90% of UCD cases present with hyaline vascular (HV) histopathology, which is characterized by atrophic germinal centers circumscribed with concentric rings of lymphocytes in an ‘onion-ring’ pattern and containing dysplastic follicular dendritic cells ; the germinal centers are penetrated by hyalinized vessels giving a ‘lollipop’ appearance. Unlike UCD, MCD is almost always symptomatic. Patients present with multifocal lymphadenopathy and signs of systemic inflammation, most commonly fever, night sweats, fluid retention, and renal dysfunction. These symptoms can be episodic, progressive, or chronic, and in severe cases can be fatal if left untreated. Laboratory tests often reveal cytopenias, abnormal liver function tests, markedly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and ESR, and proteinuria. The histopathology of MCD is more varied than UCD; it may present with a hypervascular type (hyperV), the plasmacytic (PC) type, or a mixed type. The hyperV nomenclature is used to differentiate vascular MCD from HV UCD, though HV MCD and HyperV MCD are often used interchangeably by many authors. The lymph nodes in the PC type are characterized by hypertrophic germinal centers, with intrafollicular spaces populated by sheets of plasma cells and vascular proliferations; as its name suggests, the mixed type exhibit features of both the HyperV and PC types. The etiologic agent varies for the different subtypes of MCD. Uncontrolled infection with HHV-8 is often the pathogenic driver of MCD, especially in patients who are immunocompromised due to infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In these HHV-8-associated MCD cases, CD20+ B cells act as reservoirs for HHV-8 infection and replication, with symptomology stemming from production of a viral homolog of IL-6 and subsequent downstream upregulation of proinflammatory human cytokines. For POEMS-associated MCD, up to 60% of cases are caused by malignant monoclonal plasma cells, which drive reactive lymph node changes with CD features. Cases of MCD which are not concurrent with HHV-8 infection or POEMS syndrome do not have a clear etiology and are considered idiopathic (iMCD). While the exact etiology remains unknown, IL-6 has been identified as a key pathological driver of iMCD. Episodes of disease flare may be marked by mild lymphadenopathy and B-symptoms, or in severe cases present acutely with extensive inflammation, organomegaly and organ dysfunction, pleural effusion, anasarca, and ascites. Cases of iMCD in which thrombocytopenia, anasarca, renal dysfunction or reticulin fibrosis, fever, and organomegaly are present are classified as iMCD-TAFRO. Ferritin and sCD25 are only modestly elevated in iMCD-TAFRO, whereas CRP is very high (often >100 mg/L). The gamma globulins are usually low, normal or modestly elevated in iMCD-TAFRO (5–15 g/L), in contrast to iMCD-IPL (usually >35 g/L). The cytokine profile, histopathology and clinical course of iMCD-TAFRO are different from iMCD-NOS; patients often have less markedly elevated serum IL-6 and increased serum vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), the lymph nodes are often highly vascularized and demonstrate the HyperV histopathology type, and the patients typically present with acute and severe disease. Additional differences include frequently elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) without hyperbilirubinemia or transaminase elevation, and normal to mildly elevated gammaglobulin. Differentiating iMCD-TAFRO and TAFRO syndrome is challenging due to substantial overlap of signs and symptoms and lack of specific biomarkers. While the first descriptions of TAFRO syndrome by Takai and colleagues in 2010 focused on its hyperinflammation symptoms, acute onset, and rapid progression, current perspectives now acknowledge how TAFRO presents as a constellation of nonspecific symptoms that can occur concurrently with other conditions, including malignancies, rheumatologic disorders, infections, and POEMS syndrome. Due to the heterogeneity in disease presentation, Nishimura et al. introduced the categories of probable iMCD-TAFRO and TAFRO syndrome without iMCD; these designations are based on the number of diagnostic criteria met (see below). There was an open debate as to whether TAFRO was exclusively a subtype of iMCD, a distinct clinical entity, or both. A recent retrospective analysis of data collected from 11 rheumatology and hematology centers in Japan identified 104 patients with TAFRO, of which 26 (25%) did not have lymphadenopathy, confirming that TAFRO can in fact exist without CD.

The proband, a 60-year-old male, presented to our department on January 17, 2024, with a 5-year history of elevated serum creatinine (110–160 μmol/L) and persistent proteinuria (1–2+). His medical history included long-standing hypertension and gout (duration >10 years). Notably, his family history was significant, with both his father and maternal aunt succumbing to uremia (Figure 1). Physical examination was unremarkable. The laboratory workup revealed 2+ proteinuria without hematuria, with elevated 24-h urine protein excretion of 1.1 g/24h (normal range: 0–0.15 g/24h). Serum biochemistry demonstrated normal albumin (40.5 g/L; reference 40–55 g/L), elevated creatinine (153.4 μmol/L; reference 57–111 μmol/L), and normal uric acid levels (221 μmol/L; reference 208–428 μmol/L1). Immunological profiles showed normal IgG/IgA/IgM, C3/C4 complement levels, and negative autoantibodies (ANA, dsDNA, anti-PLA2R, ANCA). Infectious disease screening was negative for HBV, HCV, HIV, syphilis, HSV, and CMV, with normal hematologic, coagulation, and thyroid function parameters. Ophthalmologic examination demonstrated no anterior lenticonus or perimacular dot/fleck retinopathy, while audiometry showed no bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Renal ultrasound revealed normal-sized kidneys with altered parenchymal echogenicity and a 2.0 × 1.6 cm right renal cyst. On light microscopy, histopathological examination showed tubulointerstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy with cystic dilatation, and global glomerulosclerosis (53%). Immunofluorescence was negative for immunoglobulins and complement. Immunohistochemistry using anti-UMOD antibody (EPR20071; Abcam) revealed abnormal intracellular accumulation of mutant uromodulin in distal tubule epithelial cells (Figure 2a and b). Electron microscopy revealed one obsolescent glomerulus with characteristic alterations: capillary endothelial vacuolization, segmental GBM thickening (250–750 nm), and diffuse podocyte foot process effacement (>80%). The mesangium showed mild hypercellularity with rare electron-dense deposits. Tubulointerstitial findings included tubular epithelial vacuolization, focal basement membrane thickening, and mild inflammatory infiltrates. Vascular changes were limited to occasional capillary erythrocyte aggregates. NGS revealed a novel heterozygous missense mutation in UMOD (NM_003361.4: c.1676A > G, p. Tyr559Cys), located within exon 8. This variant was absent from all major genomic databases (e.g. gnomAD, NCBI、OMIM, and others) and had been submitted to ClinVar with accession number RCV006253441.1. Bioinformatics analysis demonstrated that the affected tyrosine residue at position 559 was evolutionarily conserved across species (Figure 3, Ugene analysis). The patient was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3. The patient was managed with a comprehensive therapeutic regimen including valsartan (for proteinuria control), empagliflozin (for kidney protection), febuxostat (for hyperuricemia management), and sodium bicarbonate (for urine alkalization) (Table 1). At the 1-year follow-up (January 22, 2025), laboratory evaluation demonstrated stable renal function (serum creatinine 155.8 μmol/L) with significantly improved proteinuria (trace [1+] (near-normal) on urinalysis; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.29). A 36-year-old male proband presented to our department on April 7, 2024, with a 3-year history of persistently elevated serum creatinine and abnormal urinalysis. Serum creatinine fluctuated between 119 and 129 μmol/L over the past 3 years. Urinalysis demonstrated microscopic hematuria (occult blood 2+) without proteinuria. The patient had no personal history of hypertension or gout. Family history was significant for chronic kidney disease, including: (1) father with end-stage renal disease (status post renal transplantation), (2) maternal aunt with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (5-year duration), and (3) paternal grandmother who succumbed to uremia (Figure 4). Physical examination was unremarkable.

We had three cases of fetal kidneys with T2-hyperintense cortex and T2-hypointense medulla reversal of the correct appearance. In all of them, the kidneys were enlarged and hyperechoic on US of the second or third trimester, and the inverted pattern of cortex and medulla was only found on MRI. All fetuses had enlarged kidneys on MRI performed between 32 and 36 weeks (range 52–58 mm), weaker diffusion restriction in the kidneys than under normal conditions, had their bladders filled, and no oligohydramnios/anhydramnios. Figure 1 presents the MRI findings in fetus no. 1 compared with normal appearance of the fetal kidneys and with postnatal sonographic appearance. In male case no. 1, amniocentesis was performed due to the first trimester sonographic abnormalities (tricuspid valve regurgitation, regurgitation wave A, enlarged urinary bladder). The array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) analysis of the DNA extracted from uncultured amniocytes showed the deletion at 17q12 region ~ 1.4 Mb in size encompassing the region of renal cysts and diabetes (RCAD) syndrome (OMIM 137920, ORPHA: 93111). The deletion included 15 protein-coding genes, including the HNF1B gene. So far, no parental examination has been performed to assess the origin of the deletion of 17q12. At the age of 14 months, the boy’s kidney function parameters were within normal limits. In female case no. 2, there was postnatal appearance of bilateral multicystic kidney, so the PKHD1 gene was sequenced and no pathogenic variants were identified. As there was also a Müllerian duct anomaly (bicorporeal uterus with double cervix), microdeletion 17q12 syndrome was then suspected. The results of Multiplex Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification (MLPA; Kit P297-D1, MRC-Holland, Amsterdam) revealed heterozygous deletion in the region of the long arm of chromosome 17 including genes ZNHIT3, LHX1, AATF, ACACA, and HNF1B, which refers to the region typical for 17q12 microdeletion syndrome. The parents have declined testing themselves. At the age of 4.5 years, the girl has normal kidney function, and on US, the kidneys show increased cortical echogenicity, preserved cortico-medullary differentiation, and a few cortical cysts up to 4 mm. No more detailed examination of the reproductive system was performed. The same 17q12 deletion as in case no. 1 was identified postnatally in male case no. 3 using the same technique (aCGH analysis of the DNA extracted from blood). The results of MLPA in the healthy young parents are pending. Up until the age of 1 month, the boy showed no biochemical abnormalities, including kidney function parameters.

A 77-year-old man with a history of distal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction for gastric cancer presented with fever, general fatigue, and dysarthria. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed acute cerebral infarction. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus oralis, and echocardiography demonstrated vegetations on the mitral valve, leading to the diagnosis of IE. Because the vegetation showed low mobility and mitral regurgitation was not severe, conservative treatment with intravenous antibiotic therapy was initiated. Approximately 1 month later, the patient developed lower back pain, and lumbar magnetic resonance imaging revealed pyogenic spondylodiscitis (Fig 1). Concurrently, rapid morphological changes were observed in a previously diagnosed AAA, leading to the diagnosis of infected AAA with impending rupture (Fig 2). Inflammatory markers had normalized, and blood cultures had become negative, indicating clinical control of IE. Semiurgent surgical intervention for the infected AAA was required. However, the adjacent untreated spinal infection was considered to pose a high risk of graft reinfection. Therefore, a single-stage multidisciplinary surgical approach was planned. Because the patient had previously undergone robot-assisted distal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction, the availability of the greater omentum for graft coverage was uncertain. Therefore, alternative reconstructive options, including a rectus abdominis muscle flap, were considered preoperatively. During adhesiolysis, a viable residual omentum was identified and preserved for graft coverage. The vascular surgery team performed complete resection of infected aortic tissue followed by in situ reconstruction using a rifampicin-soaked prosthetic graft. The graft was routed through a pathway separate from the infected spinal field, representing an infection-avoiding graft-routing strategy (Fig 3). After extensive irrigation, the orthopedic surgery team performed L4/5 discectomy, curettage, and resection of the necrotic vertebral end plate, followed by anterior spinal reconstruction using an autologous iliac crest bone graft without instrumentation (Fig 4). The anterior vertebral periosteum was closed to the extent feasible to separate the spinal field from the vascular graft. The graft was repeatedly irrigated intraoperatively and finally covered with the omental flap. Intraoperative cultures from the aneurysm, vertebral body, and intervertebral disc showed no growth of pathogenic organisms. Postoperatively, the patient developed chylous ascites, which subsequently resolved with temporary abdominal drainage and conservative management. No recurrence of infection was observed, and the patient was discharged approximately 3 months after surgery with continued oral antibiotic therapy (Fig 5).

An 8-year-old child presented to Nauru Medical Center with cough and failure to thrive. The child was born to a 36-year-old G3P3 mother via normal vaginal delivery after a previous cesarean section. Shortly after birth, the infant developed neonatal cyanosis, which initially resolved but later recurred, resulting in a 3-month admission to the neonatal intensive care unit, where oxygen therapy was required. At the age of 3 months, a CT scan of the chest suggested the presence of only a functioning left lung. During early childhood, the patient was considered medically fragile and required home oxygen therapy until the age of 2 years. Despite early concerns regarding possible long-term disability, the child achieved all developmental milestones appropriately. Since the age of 2 years, the patient has remained clinically stable, with no hospital admissions and only 1-2 minor respiratory illnesses per year, which were managed in the outpatient department. The child currently attends regular school and is in Grade 2. The parents reported a history of recurrent respiratory infections since infancy, occasionally associated with symptoms suggestive of cardiac failure. These episodes required hospitalization on 1 occasion for 1 month, during which the patient was treated conservatively. Before the arrival of a new medical team from GMSS, Nauru Medical Center did not have specialist medical services available. The parents denied any history of tuberculosis, hepatitis, or other chronic infectious diseases. They also denied any drug or food allergies. There was no history of chills, vomiting, diarrhea, or convulsions. On physical examination, the child appeared comfortable at rest. Oxygen saturation on room air was 88%, likely reflecting chronic adaptation to long-standing hypoxemia. The most notable finding was digital clubbing involving the toes. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations showed an elevated hemoglobin level of 17.6 g/dL, above the normal range, likely to represent secondary polycythemia due to chronic hypoxemia. Other laboratory parameters were within normal limits, including white blood cell count, red blood cell count, neutrophil count and percentage, lymphocyte ratio, and platelet count. Additional investigations, including liver function tests, renal function tests, and immunoglobulin levels, were also normal. The patient was referred to the radiology department for further cardiac evaluation and underwent transthoracic echocardiography. Echocardiography demonstrated marked cardiac displacement to the right side hemithorax with preserved normal leftward apex orientation and situs solitus (cardiac dextroposition), along with right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation of the right atrium and IVC (Fig. 1). About 8 mm in size an ASD was also identified, showing a bidirectional shunt more form right to left consistent with advanced pulmonary vascular disease. There was a large PDA and a dilated main pulmonary artery with pulmonary HTN measuring 44 mmHg. The PDA demonstrated bidirectional flow on color Doppler imaging. The left pulmonary veins drained into the left atrium, but the right pulmonary veins were not visualized draining into the left atrium. Instead, they appeared to course inferiorly and join the IVC, raising strong suspicion for anomalous pulmonary venous return with complex congenital cardiac anomalies and advanced pulmonary hypertension resulting in Eisenmenger syndrome. A chest radiograph was subsequently performed. This showed a significant reduction in right lung volume with rightward mediastinal shift and relative hyperinflation of the left lung.

A 58-year-old man presented with recurrent bleeding from a permanent ileal conduit urostomy. His medical history was notable for bladder and prostate cancer treated with cystoprostatectomy and ileal conduit urinary diversion 2 years prior to presentation. Additional comorbidities included obesity (BMI 37 kg/m²), chronic kidney disease stage 3, prior venous thromboembolism on anticoagulation, and cirrhosis secondary to metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with ongoing alcohol use. The patient experienced multiple hospital admissions over an 18-month period for recurrent episodes of gross hematuria via the urostomy, resulting in symptomatic anemia requiring repeated blood transfusions. He described steady, nonpulsatile bleeding from the stoma associated with fatigue and dyspnea. Social history was significant for continued alcohol consumption of approximately 3-6 beers daily with heavier intake on weekends. On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 127/79 mmHg, heart rate 84 bpm). The urostomy appliance contained gross blood. There was no ascites, jaundice, or hepatic encephalopathy. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL), preserved hepatic synthetic function (albumin 3.9 g/dL, INR 1.1), and chronic kidney disease (creatinine 2.0 mg/dL). The Model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) score was 12, and Child–Pugh class was A. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated hepatic steatosis, mild splenomegaly, and prominent stomal venous collaterals extending from the right superficial inferior epigastric vein to the ileal conduit, consistent with stomal varices (Fig. 1). Transhepatic portal venography confirmed portal hypertension with a portosystemic pressure gradient of 12 mmHg and demonstrated stomal varices draining into superficial abdominal wall veins (Fig. 2). Endoscopic evaluation of the ileal conduit revealed mucosal congestion and vascular ectasia consistent with portal hypertensive enteropathy (PHE), as well as small grade I varices approximately 2 cm from the stoma without high-risk stigmata (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Correlation of imaging, venography, and endoscopic findings established the diagnosis of urostomy-associated stomal variceal bleeding secondary to portal hypertension. Initial management consisted of direct percutaneous puncture of the stomal varices under fluoroscopic guidance. Venography confirmed variceal anatomy, and embolosclerotherapy was performed using 2 cc of sodium tetradecyl sulfate (STS) mixed with 6 cc of air, followed by Gelfoam slurry. This resulted in transient hemostasis. Bleeding recurred after 4 weeks, with active hemorrhage visualized at the urostomy stoma. A transhepatic portal venous approach was subsequently pursued, and embolization of the stomal varices was performed using 0.018-inch detachable coils and Gelfoam (Fig. 5). Despite technical success, bleeding again recurred 6 weeks later. Given prior evidence recommending carvedilol for treatment of increased hepatic vascular resistance, nonselective beta-blockade with carvedilol 6.25 mg twice daily was initiated for 6 weeks. Despite achieving adequate heart rate reduction (66 bpm), intermittent bleeding persisted. Due to the failure of local and embolization-based therapies, portal decompression was pursued. A TIPS was placed via a transjugular approach, reducing the portosystemic gradient from 15 mmHg to 9 mmHg (Fig. 6). Following TIPS placement, the patient developed hepatic encephalopathy 1 week postprocedure, requiring hospitalization and initiation of lactulose and rifaximin. Symptoms resolved within 48 hours, and the patient was discharged home. At 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-up, Doppler ultrasound demonstrated a patent TIPS with normal flow velocities, and the patient reported no further episodes of urostomy bleeding.

A previously healthy 4-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with intermittent abdominal pain and episodic non-bilious vomiting of several weeks’ duration. The pain was colicky, recurrent, and poorly localized. There was no history of fever, weight loss, trauma, prior abdominal surgery, or exposure to livestock or unpasteurized dairy products. On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable. The abdomen was mildly distended but soft, without guarding or rebound tenderness. No palpable mass was identified. Laboratory investigations were largely unremarkable. The white blood cell count was within normal limits without leukocytosis. Mild anemia was noted on subsequent testing. Platelet count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Tumor markers (AFP and β-hCG) were normal. Echinococcus serology was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a left paracolic gutter fluid collection with multiple well defined internal components which could represent daughter cysts. Additional findings included reactive mesenteric lymph nodes (largest approximately 1 × 0.8 cm), displacement of adjacent bowel loops without evidence of obstruction, and mild surrounding inflammatory changes. No definite communication with adjacent bowel loops was identified on CT. Based on these imaging features, hydatid disease was initially suspected. (Fig. 1, Fig. 2). Follow-up MRI demonstrated interval migration of the lesion from the left paracolic gutter to the right lower quadrant, indicating lesion mobility. The lesion showed heterogeneous signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images with multiple internal floating rounded components. Focal internal calcification was present. Post-contrast images demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement with adjacent mesenteric stranding and persistent mild intraperitoneal free fluid. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no definite restricted diffusion. The interval positional change raised strong suspicion for bowel-related pathology rather than a fixed peritoneal cyst (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6, Fig. 7). The patient underwent surgical exploration. An inflamed Meckel’s diverticulum arising from the ileum was identified and resected. Enterolith formation surrounding the foreign body. The presumed daughter cysts on imaging corresponded to inflammatory debris and enterolith fragments within the fluid-filled diverticulum.

A 58-year-old woman with a past medical history of uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis treated medically in the past and remote caesarean section, presented to the emergency department with 3 days of left lower quadrant pain. An imaging and interventional overview of the patient’s hospital course can be reviewed in Fig. An IV contrast enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis in portal venous phase with coronal and sagittal reconstruction was obtained, employing iterative dose reduction technique (CECT). This demonstrated acute perforated sigmoid diverticulitis without abscess. The patient was admitted for IV antibiotics, fluids and pain control, and discharged the next day. However, the patient continued to have gradually increasing pain, and prompted by new fecal urgency, returned to ED 2 days after discharge. On examination, the patient was tender to palpation in the LLQ without rebound, and afebrile with white cell count (WCC) of 10. Portal venous phase CECT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3 cm collection contiguous with inflamed sigmoid diverticula, involving the ovary and a gas-filled serpiginous structure, the left fallopian tube (Fig. 1). This was consistent with perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with abscess and the rare finding of pneumosalpinx. The patient was admitted to surgery. Interventional radiology was enlisted to drain the collection on the day of admission. Nonenhanced CT biopsy was conducted. A narrow window was identified between the broad ligament ovarian vessels and the iliac artery and vein was identified, whereupon an 18-gauge Chiba needle advanced inferior to the broad ligament until the needle tip was within the collection and 10 cc purulent material was aspirated. Passed via wire, a 10 French cope loop drainage catheter was placed in the collection with near complete resolution (Fig. 3). IV broad spectrum antibiotics were continued. WCC trended down over subsequent days and patient tolerated a diet, but began to require increasing pain control, prompting CECT of the abdomen and pelvis on day 5 of admission. This revealed resolution of the drained abscess but interval progression of multiple abscesses in the region of the sigmoid and mesentery (Fig. 4). Monitoring continued. Due to persistent elevated WCC, unremitting pain and progression of collections, patient was taken to OR day 6 following admission. Robotic sigmoid colectomy, end colostomy (Hartmann's procedure), and drainage of intra-abdominal abscesses was performed by general surgery. Hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (THBSO) was performed by gynecologic surgery. Intraoperatively the left adnexa was noted to be adherent to a pelvic collection and to a portion of sigmoid colon, with fistulous communication. IR drain was removed. A Blake drain was placed in the largest collection in the right lower quadrant and removed before discharge following an unremarkable postoperative course. OR wound cultures obtained on antibiotics were positive for candida albicans and fluconazole was added to the outpatient regimen. Surgical pathology confirmed fallopian tubes showing florid bilateral salpingitis with abscess, and fibrinous adhesions with pyogenic material (Fig. 6). Robotic assisted colostomy reversal (reversal of Hartmann's) was performed successfully 4 months following the surgery.

A 38-year-old woman initially presented with bloating and abdominal pain and was found to have large bilateral ovarian masses on outside imaging. She underwent resections at an outside institution resulting in mature teratomas. Her symptoms returned 3 years later with recurrent right ovarian lesion at an outside institution. Right salpingo-oophorectomy resulted in recurrent teratoma. Follow-up imaging at the outside institution showed multiple peritoneal masses that were biopsied and found to be strumosis without atypia. The timeline of important clinical events is outlined in Fig. Four years after her initial symptoms, she presented to our institution for additional workup and treatment due to relocation. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple enhancing peritoneal and abdominal wall masses and a homogenously enhancing structure in the left adnexa which was favored to represent the ovary (Fig. 2). The abdominal wall masses were biopsied and demonstrated follicular thyroid tissue without atypia. At this time, the patient had a markedly elevated thyroglobulin level of 4326 ng/mL (normal range 1.6-50 ng/mL). An I-123 whole body scan utilizing 1.2mCi of I-123 was administered to the patient, who was placed on a low iodine diet prior to the exam. The 24-hour uptake scan showed significant uptake in the thyroid, but no significant uptake in the multiple peritoneal and abdominal wall lesions. This finding may have been due to the uptake of the majority of the radiotracer by the thyroid gland (Fig. 4A). Five years after her initial presentation, the patient underwent a round of cytoreductive surgery in the abdomen and pelvis, resulting in a lowering of the thyroglobulin level of 335.5 ng/mL. Several months after the cytoreductive surgery, she underwent total thyroidectomy, which further lowered the thyroglobulin level to 205 ng/mL. She then underwent a second round of cytoreductive surgery in the abdomen and pelvis with removal of multiple peritoneal masses including a mass in the left ovary. Pathological examination demonstrated well-differentiated follicular thyroid tissue (Fig. 3). The patient was reimaged using 3.4 mCi of I-123 (Fig. 4B), and a 24-hour uptake scan showed uptake in the remnant thyroid tissue in the thyroid bed. Shortly thereafter, given patient’s persistent elevated thyroglobulin levels, patient underwent radioiodine therapy with 128 mCi of I-131 with 7-day post ablation imaging demonstrating I-131 uptake within multiple sites in the abdomen and pelvis (Fig. 4C). Over the next two years, her thyroglobulin levels decreased substantially with mild interval fluctuations, with the most recent level at 57.4 ng/mL. However, the most recent follow-up surveillance MRI showed small enhancing foci suspicious for early recurrent disease within the peritoneal cavity. There has been no post-surgical MRI or CT demonstrating a confirmed disease-free state during surveillance follow-up.

A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis. Notably, she has a personal history of TSC and seizures. She has a family history of TSC with multiple siblings and father diagnosed with the condition; however, they were not afflicted with an arterial pathology. On physical examination, there were multiple hyperpigmented macules, ash leaf spots, fascial fibromas, and extremity fibromas. The abdomen was diffusely tender with focal peritonitis along the midline with an obvious pulsatile mass. Vital signs showed tachycardia to 120 beats per minute, hypertension (180/90 mm Hg), and adequate oxygenation on room air. Her vascular examination was intact with bilateral palpable femoral, radial, and pedal pulses. Axial and coronal computed tomography angiography demonstrated an isolated 7.2-cm retroperitoneally contained a ruptured I-AAA (Fig 1, Fig 2, Fig 3). Impulse control was promptly initiated to lessen further exsanguination risk and the patient was transported emergently to the operating room for open repair of the ruptured I-AAA. Laparotomy revealed a 7.2-cm purely I-AAA with contained rupture into the retroperitoneum. A transperitoneal approach was undertaken given the left lateral retroperitoneal nature of the rupture. This strategy allowed appropriate aortic control distal to the bilateral renal arteries before aortic transection. Transperitoneal infrarenal aortic and bilateral common iliac artery control were obtained swiftly. The patient was heparinized in the standard fashion. Aortotomy, lumbar artery ligation, and appropriate hemostasis were performed. Notably, the radiographically identified posterior left lateral rupture site was easily confirmed on examination of the aneurysmal aortic wall (Fig 4). The infrarenal to aortic bifurcation was then reconstructed with an 14-mm diameter tubular polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) graft tailored to an appropriate length for optimal interpositioning. Moreover, we anticipated the need for a long-term and slightly oversized graft option that would be suitable for decades of use. As such, after expert discussion, we elected to use the PTFE tubular graft platform to perform our aortic reconstruction. Although Dacron (Invista) is certainly a reasonable option, we believed that PTFE would afford the patient a more durable repair. The graft was sewn in place and buttressed with felt pledgeting proximally and distally. Graft felt pledgeting was used to reinforce anastomoses because we knew these anastomoses would certainly evolve and potentially degenerate with normal adolescent development. The aortic aneurysm sac was further closed around the graft. The patient was noted to have palpable femoral and pedal pulses before closing the abdomen in the standard fashion. The patient was then admitted to the surgical intensive care unit postoperatively. The patient was extubated within 24 hours postoperatively and experienced a largely uneventful hospital course, with discharge to the neighboring children's hospital on postoperative day 4. Repeat computed tomography angiography was performed before discharge, which demonstrated an intact I-AAA repair without major surgical concern. She was ultimately discharged home on postoperative day 7. At the 3-month postoperative follow-up visit, she was noted to have recovered well from surgery and planned for 6-month interval imaging. Patient consent for publication was obtained per institution protocol.

This is a 42-year-old male who was involved in a motor vehicle collision. At the scene, he was found in respiratory distress with a deep, irregular respiratory rate of twenty breaths per minute and a low Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score, likely due to alcohol intoxication. Consequently, he was intubated at the scene and transported to the trauma room. Upon examination in the trauma room, he had a GCS score of 2T/15, which indicated severe impairment, and bilateral 3 mm reactive pupils, suggesting initially intact brainstem function despite the severe condition. Under the effects of a muscle relaxant and sedation, the chest examination revealed decreased air entry on the left side, while the FAST exam was negative. A CT scan showed multiple left-sided rib fractures with underlying pulmonary contusions, mild hemothorax, and pneumothorax, with no abnormalities in the head CT scan (Fig. 1), abdomen, and pelvis. The ethanol level was 65.1 mmol/l, reflecting significant intoxication at the time of the incident. He was subsequently admitted to the trauma ICU. A follow-up CT head the next day (Fig. 2) revealed a small extra-axial hematoma, a few scattered small hemorrhagic contusions, and minimal subarachnoid hemorrhage. Due to persistent low GCS, an MRI on day 3 showed a diffuse axonal injury grade 3. The patient was started on DVT prophylaxis and maintained on levetiracetam 500mg, initiated at admission. A subsequent CT scan the next day showed no significant changes. Due to persistently low GCS, he underwent percutaneous dilatation tracheostomy on the seventh day of his admission. Over the following week, his GCS improved to E3M6Vt. He was tolerating a tracheal mask. Over the next 10 days, his conscious level improved further, with a GCS of E4M6 Vt. On the 19th of his admission, in the evening, he suddenly became unresponsive with fixed dilated pupils with no corneal reflex but preserved cough reflex. There was no witnessed or suspected fall, and no abnormal behavior or agitation before the incident. The patient underwent emergency CT head showing newly developed right-sided cerebral convexity SDH with diffuse edema, with midline shift of 7.5 mm toward the left side and crowding at the foramen magnum with tonsillar herniation (Fig. 3). He underwent emergency right decompressive craniectomy and evacuation of acute SDH (Fig. 4). The presumed source of the hematoma was the cortical vein, which was identified and coagulated. After returning from the operating room, on examination, his pupils were fixed and dilated, with no corneal or cough reflex. He underwent a follow-up CT scan of the head that showed findings suggestive of multiple foci of ischemic changes, diffuse edema, and brainstem hemorrhage. The next day, the patient was polyuric with a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. As he lost the brain stem reflexes, the brain stem testing confirmed brain death on the third day of the event.

A 51-year-old male presented with complaints of abdominal pain for the past 1 month, which had progressively increased in severity and was not relieved by medications. The pain was associated with nausea and vomiting. He was a known case of hypertension for 1 year and diabetes mellitus for 5 years with a history of occasional alcohol intake over the past 20 years. The patient also reported episodic headache, palpitations, and weight loss. Routine blood investigations revealed elevated serum amylase (∼725 U/L) and serum lipase (∼583 U/L), along with raised total leukocyte count (∼19.9 × 10³/µL). A diagnosis of acute pancreatitis was made, and the patient was referred to the radiology department for contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to assess for complications of pancreatitis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen performed on a 64-slice scanner revealed multiple cystic lesions in the liver, pancreas, and bilateral kidneys. Imaging revealed near-complete replacement of pancreatic parenchyma with multiple variable-sized cystic lesions. The entire left adrenal gland was replaced by a multiloculated cystic lesion with a small enhancing solid component. In addition, features of pancreatitis were present, including peripancreatic, perirenal, and bilateral paracolic gutter fat stranding with a few loculated collections in the lesser sac and perisplenic region. Mild prominence of the pancreatic duct was noted without evidence of pancreatic calcification. A provisional radiological diagnosis of acute-on-chronic pancreatitis with walled-off necrosis was made in the background of suspected VHL, with an associated mixed solid-cystic left adrenal lesion, likely representing a cystic pheochromocytoma. Biochemical evaluation was performed and revealed mildly elevated plasma-free normetanephrine levels (526.9 pg/mL) with normal plasma-free metanephrine levels. Owing to its atypical predominantly cystic appearance and the need for definitive tissue diagnosis, CT-guided biopsy of the left adrenal lesion was performed under appropriate hemodynamic precautions, with emergency support and interventional radiology backup readily available. Histopathological examination revealed nests (zellballen pattern) of polygonal tumor cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma. Areas of cystic degeneration and hemorrhage were identified, correlating with the imaging appearance. Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin, confirming the diagnosis of cystic pheochromocytoma.

A 15-year-old male presented to the Internal Medicine Clinic of the Thalassaemia and Congenital Blood Diseases Center (Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region, Iraq) on September, 2021 with complaints of colicky abdominal pain, episodic severe dysentery (>10 times a day) for a period of 6 years, and fatigue for 2 months. He had been receiving regular blood transfusions since he was diagnosed with thalassemia major at 1 year of age. Chelation therapy had been required since the age of 5 years. When the patient was 8 years of age, he experienced intermittent abdominal pain, dysentery and weight loss. A general stool examination (GSE) was performed at that time and revealed Entamoeba histolytica (E. histolytica) infection. The patient received metronidazole. However, 4 years thereafter, the patient was diagnosed with growth failure and treated with growth hormone (GH) replacement therapy for 1 year, although there was no response to the treatment. Clinical findings. Upon a physical examination, he had a typical thalassemic face (frontal bossing and flattened nasal bridge), jaundice, tachycardia (110 bpm) and a slightly distended abdomen. Diagnostic assessment. Blood analyses revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin level, 50 g/l), an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level (265 mg/l), a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (120 mm/h) and a negative Coombs test. He had an infection with E. histolytica according to the GSE, and the fecal calprotectin level was elevated (>1,000 µg/g). The patient was referred to a pediatric gastroenterologist, who performed a colonoscopy and obtained biopsies. The histopathological analysis of the specimens confirmed the diagnosis of CD (data not shown as images could not be retrieved). Therapeutic intervention. The patient was treated with mercaptopurine (25 mg/day), mesalazine (2 g/day, suppository) and prednisolone (20 mg/day). After 1 month, the patient developed cholestatic jaundice, and the use of mercaptopurine was terminated; however, the patient's condition worsened. A magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography scan revealed sclerosing cholangitis (Fig. 1), and he was treated with ursodeoxycholic acid (13-15 mg/kg/day, divided into 2-3 doses for a lifetime duration). The patient remained under follow-up for the monitoring of cholangitis. The frequency of diarrhea decreased to three to five episodes per day, and the hemoglobin level increased to 80 g/l. Unfortunately, the patient's cholangitis progressively worsened, leading to jaundice and sepsis. Despite treatment, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and the patient succumbed ~2 years after the initial presentation. A 13-year-old female patient presented with thalassemia major to the Thalassaemia and Congenital Blood Diseases Center (Sulaymaniyah, Iraq) on September, 2021 with severe dysentery (more than 8 times/day), colicky abdominal pain, fatigue and increasing pallor. The patient had been on regular transfusions since 3 months of age and commenced chelation at the age of 3 years. At the age of 11 years, she was diagnosed with growth failure and underwent 1 year of GH replacement therapy without significant improvement. She reported a history of intermittent abdominal pain, weight loss and bloody diarrhea for 3 years. On each occasion, GSE tested positive for E. histolytica, for which she had been prescribed antibiotics by a gastroenterologist. Recently, the patient's condition had begun to deteriorate further. Clinical findings. A physical examination revealed that she had a typical thalassemic facial appearance characterized by frontal bossing, a flattened nasal bridge and jaundice. Diagnostic assessment.

A 16-year-old female with no previous comorbidities presented with dyspnea, odynophagia, and hemoptysis-associated cough. She was from a rural area in Maranhão, a state of autochthonous OROV transmission located near the Brazilian Amazon region, and denied recent travel. She sought emergency care, two days after onset of symptoms, where a chest X-ray suggested pneumonia, resulting in her hospitalization. Her condition progressively worsened on the next day, with increased dyspnea and cough accompanied by headache and right-sided chest pain. Orotracheal intubation was performed on the third day of illness, when massive bleeding through the endotracheal tube was identified. The patient had a hemodynamic worsening, and subsequently died. The autopsy revealed a bilateral large serosanguineous pleural effusion totaling approximately one liter. The lungs exhibited a purplish color with hemorrhagic spots; cut surfaces showed congestion and hemorrhage; petechiae were diffusely distributed in the pericardium, along with mild cerebral edema and tonsillar herniation. Microscopic findings showed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and pulmonary edema (Fig. 1). The kidneys showed acute tubular necrosis with vascular congestion. The liver exhibited only vascular congestion. Samples were collected for reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction testing for arboviruses and respiratory viruses. Results were positive for OROV and H1N1. For the complete list of infectious agents tested, see Table 1. For the other infectious agents, the results were negative.

Patient 1 was a 62-year-old female with a history of class 1 obesity (pre-treatment BMI 34.0 kg m−2) and hypertension and no prior history of depression or mood disorders. The patient had lost 26% of her weight while being treated with subcutaneous tirzepatide over the course of 19 months, up to a dose of 15 mg·week−1. The patient joined our online clinic to help optimize her body composition and overall health. Our clinicians introduced her to strength training and recommended dietary changes. Patient 2 was a 36-year-old female with a history of class 1 obesity (pre-treatment BMI 33.9 kg m−2) along with depression and anxiety. The patient had lost 23% of her weight while being treated with 15 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide over the previous 24 months. She had previously used bupropion but had not taken it for several years. The patient joined our online clinic after seeing an online discussion of potential anhedonia precipitated by tirzepatide use. Patient 3 was a 64-year-old female with a history of class 3 obesity (pre-treatment BMI 49.9 kg m−2) and no history of depression or mood disorders. The patient had lost 57% of her weight while being treated with 15 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide. The patient was not aware of subjective mood disturbances at this point. Patient 1 described feeling a lack of motivation to exercise and loss of interest in her other hobbies. Patient 2 described feeling “flat” and unmotivated despite her weight loss success. She noted that these feelings differed from her feelings when previously diagnosed with depression. The patient also described being aware that she should exercise but being unable to “get herself to do it.” Patient 3 briefly stopped tirzepatide due to a medical procedure. The timeline for each patient is displayed in Fig. Patient 1 was interviewed concerning past and current tirzepatide treatment, weight loss, and current lack of motivation and loss of interest in hobbies. Patient 2 was interviewed concerning past and current tirzepatide treatment, weight loss, history of depression, past bupropion use, and current feelings of “flatness.” Patient 3 was interviewed concerning past and current tirzepatide treatment, weight loss, and changes in medication use surrounding her medical procedure. In all cases, the presence of anhedonia was assessed through patient screening and clinical history taking. Anhedonia was established based on the loss of pleasure in previously rewarding experiences after ruling out organic or biological causes (e.g., hormonal, anemia, nutritional deficiencies, and sleep disturbances) and signs of depression other than anhedonia. Patient 1 was prescribed a reduced dose of 10 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide for four months, during which the patient's desire to exercise and continue past hobbies improved markedly. Patient 2 was prescribed a reduced dose of 10 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide for four weeks, during which she noticed significant improvements in her “flat” feelings but did not experience full resolution. At that point, 150 mg·day−1 bupropion XL was prescribed, which further improved her feelings within several weeks. Patient 3 was required to temporarily stop her medication due to a procedure and resumed tirzepatide at a dose of 7.5 mg·week−1. Following the initial resolution of anhedonia, Patient 1 chose to self-administer a 12.5 mg·week−1 dose of subcutaneous tirzepatide for two months, followed by a 15 mg·week−1 dose for an additional two months, due to frustration with stalled weight loss. During this time, the patient's lack of motivation quickly returned, and no further weight loss was achieved. At this point, the patient was transitioned back to 10 mg·week−1 tirzepatide for four months, which resulted in improved motivation but some continued “flatness.” As such, the dose was further reduced to 5 mg·week−1 tirzepatide for four additional months.

A 9-year-old Indonesian male presented to the Center for Biomedical Research, Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Diponegoro (Semarang, Indonesia) with a history of multiple fractures, skeletal deformities, and joint contractures. He was born to a 28-year-old mother (G2P1A0) following an uncomplicated and healthy pregnancy. No infections, complications, or use of unprescribed medications were reported during gestation. At birth, his weight was 2.8 kg and his length was 49 cm. The family is non-consanguineous, with no known history of genetic or hereditary disorders (Fig. 1). The patient sustained his first fracture, a femoral break, at the age of one. Since then, he has experienced a total of eleven fractures, the most recent being an open humeral fracture at the age of eight. Clinical examination revealed blue sclera, DI, and bottle caries. There were no signs of facial dysmorphism, hearing loss, or visual impairment. Audiometric and tympanometry assessments confirmed normal hearing. Musculoskeletal evaluation showed elbow and wrist contractures, acetabular hypermobility with deformity, sternal and rib deformities, and kyphosis (Fig. 1). Additionally, the patient exhibited gross motor developmental delay, microcephaly (Z score − 2.81), severe underweight (Z score − 7.4), and short stature (Z score − 7.18), likely secondary to skeletal abnormalities and joint contractures. The skeletal survey revealed generalized osteopenia, Wormian bones in the skull, spinal platyspondyly, acetabular protrusion, and multiple skeletal deformities. These included evidence of old fractures involving the right posterior 5th–9th ribs and the proximal to midshaft region of the left ulna. Genetic testing using the targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) custom-made OI-related gene panel was performed. The analysis identified compound heterozygous NM_182943.3(PLOD2):c.880-1G > C, p.? and NM_182943.3(PLOD2):c.1559dupC, p.(Val523Cysfs*7) variants in the PLOD2 gene (Fig. 2). Compound heterozygosity for these variants was confirmed by Sanger sequence analysis in the parents: the mother was a heterozygous carrier of the c.1559dupC variant, while the c.880-1G > C was identified in the father (Fig. 2). The c.880-1G > C splice site variant affects the consensus sequence of intron 8 acceptor sites. As such, in silico this variant is predicted to abolish the acceptor site (Splice AI score for acceptor loss = 0.96, Splice-Altering / Strong). One potential effect of this variant is the skipping of the nearby located exon 9, leading to an in-frame deletion of 42 amino acids (p.Val294_Lys335del). This deletion concerns several amino acid residues predicted to undergo post-translational modifications, as reported in UniProt. The variant is absent in control population databases (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/v.4.1) and the OI Leiden Open Variation Database (LOVD) database, indicating it as a novel undescribed variant. This variant is classified as likely pathogenic according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria (PVS1_Mod, PM2_Supp, PM3, PP4). Variant classification was performed using the MANE Select transcript NM_182943.3 (PLOD2), and ACMG criteria were applied according to standard guidelines, with PVS1 applied at a moderate level due to uncertainty in the predicted splicing effect. The c.1559dupC is a frameshift variant in exon 14, introducing a premature stop codon. This variant has been previously reported in homozygous state in two index patients affected with BRKS2 and in compound heterozygosity with a missense variant in a patient with BRKS2. It is rare in population databases (Grpmax Filtering Allele Frequency (95% confidence) = 0.000018; gnomadAD Browser, v.4.1). It is classified as pathogenic based on ACMG guidelines (PVS1, PM2_Supp, PM3_Strong, PP4). Based on clinical presentation and molecular findings, the patient was diagnosed with BRKS2.

Case 1 was a 34‐year‐old woman born to nonconsanguineous parents, with normal birth, neurodevelopment, academic performance, and preserved cognition. At 13 years of age, she developed a symmetrical upper limb rest tremor. Over subsequent years, she experienced slowly progressive weakness predominantly affecting the lower limbs, with clear proximal predominance. From symptom onset, she reported disproportionate difficulty with activities requiring hip flexion, including climbing stairs, rising from a seated position, and getting into a car. Upper limb involvement emerged later, predominantly affecting arm extension and hand dexterity. Neurological examination at 25 years of age showed a waddling gait and Gowers' sign. Using the 0–5 Medical Research Council (MRC) scale demonstrated symmetric, nonlength‐dependent weakness: neck flexion 5, neck extension 5; arm abduction 3, arm adduction 4; elbow flexion 4+, elbow extension 2–3; wrist flexion 4, wrist extension 4+; finger extension 4, intrinsic hand muscles 4; hip flexion 2, hip extension 3; leg adduction 4+, leg abduction 4+; knee extension 3, knee flexion 4−; ankle dorsiflexion 2, ankle plantar flexion 2; toe extension 2, and toe flexion 2. Deep tendon reflexes were preserved in the upper limbs and absent in the lower limbs. A mild rest tremor was present without bradykinesia or rigidity. Sensory examination, cranial nerve examination, cognition, and fundoscopy were normal, with no cherry‐red macula, psychiatric or extrapyramidal features. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated normal sensory nerve action potentials and reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes in the lower limbs. Electromyography in both upper and lower limbs showed diffuse chronic denervation with a proximal and non–length‐dependent distribution. MLPA analysis revealed two copies of SMN1. Case 2 was a 32‐year‐old woman born to nonconsanguineous parents, with normal birth, neurodevelopment, and preserved cognitive function. At 15 years of age, she developed a mild, symmetrical, bilateral resting tremor affecting the upper limbs. In subsequent years, she experienced slowly progressive, predominantly proximal weakness, more marked in the lower limbs. Similar to Case 1, she reported difficulties performing activities dependent on hip flexion. In early adulthood, she developed frequent falls, becoming wheelchair dependent for long distances by 21 years of age. Upper limb weakness emerged later, at age 25, predominantly affecting arm extension. Neurological examination at 19 years of age revealed a highly similar pattern of non–length‐dependent weakness, as shown in power examination graded by the 0–5 MRC scale: neck flexion 5, neck extension 5; arm abduction 3, arm adduction 4; elbow flexion 4+, elbow extension 2–3; wrist flexion 4, wrist extension 4+; finger extension 4, intrinsic hand muscles 4; hip flexion 2, hip extension 3; leg adduction 4+, leg abduction 4+; knee extension 3, knee flexion 4−; ankle dorsiflexion 2, ankle plantar flexion 2; toe extension 2, and toe flexion 2. Deep tendon reflexes, sensory, cranial nerve, cognitive, and extrapyramidal examinations were normal. Whole‐exome sequencing (WES) in Case 1 identified two heterozygous HEXA variants (NM_000520.6): c.533G>A (p.Arg178His) and c.782G>A (p.Gly261Asp). The p.Arg178His variant is classified as pathogenic in ClinVar and has been repeatedly reported in TSD, including attenuated phenotypes, both in homozygosity and compound heterozygosity, consistently associated with late‐onset or subacute forms rather than infantile disease. The p.Gly261Asp variant affects a conserved residue, is predicted deleterious by in silico tools, and is absent in homozygosity in gnomAD v4. Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation in trans, supporting compound heterozygosity. β‐Hexosaminidase analysis demonstrated mildly reduced absolute HexA activity (500.0 nmol/h/mL; reference 550–1675), reduced total hexosaminidase activity, and preserved relative HexA fraction (62%), consistent with partial HexA deficiency. In Case 2, WES identified two heterozygous HEXA variants: c.1495C>T (p.Arg499Cys) and c.805G>A (p.Gly269Ser), both classified as pathogenic in ClinVar and affecting conserved residues. β‐Hexosaminidase analysis showed markedly reduced absolute HexA activity (129 nmol/h/mL; reference 550–1675), reduced total hexosaminidase activity, and a reduced relative HexA fraction (38%), confirming partial HexA deficiency. wbMRI in both patients demonstrated a symmetric pattern of selective fatty infiltration on T1‐weighted sequences with normal STIR imaging, indicating a chronic, noninflammatory process. Fatty infiltration predominantly affected the triceps brachii in the upper limbs; the iliopsoas, gluteus medius, and gluteus minimus at the pelvic level; and anterior and posterior compartments of the thighs and legs, with relative sparing of the adductor longus, semitendinosus, and, to a lesser extent, toe extensors (Figure 1).

A 42-year-old female presented to the emergency department with massive gross hematuria approximately 40 days following an uncomplicated right percutaneous nephrolithotomy procedure. Upon admission, the patient was hemodynamically unstable, exhibiting signs of significant blood loss. Laboratory findings revealed a substantial drop in hemoglobin levels, necessitating the transfusion of 11 packed red blood cell units in the whole course of admission. After initial stabilization, computed tomography angiography was performed to identify the source of bleeding, revealing a renal artery pseudoaneurysm (Fig. 1). Given the severity of the hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability, arterial angioembolization was attempted. However, this intervention proved unsuccessful in achieving definitive hemostasis. Due to the persistent, massive gross hematuria and the failure of angioembolization, a decision was made for immediate surgical intervention. The patient was positioned prone under general anesthesia. The collecting system was opacified through retrograde contrast injection under fluoroscopy to identify the calyx containing pseudoaneurysm. Percutaneous antegrade access to the target calyx was then obtained under fluoroscopic guidance. Preoperative imaging was correlated with intraoperative fluoroscopic findings to identify the target calyx and to selecting the most appropriate access tract accordingly. Upon endoscopic exploration, a renal artery pseudoaneurysm was identified. After identification of the pseudoaneurysm and evacuation of intrarenal clots, the bleeding source was clearly visualized as an actively bleeding arterial branch within the pseudo aneurysmal cavity. Under continuous direct endoscopic visualization, a standard monopolar transurethral resection system, routinely used for transurethral resection of bladder tumors (TURB), was introduced into the renal collecting system (Fig. 2). Hemostasis was achieved using a TURB loop electrode, applying a technique analogous to conventional bladder tumor resection, with appropriate adaptation to the intrarenal anatomy. Controlled and stepwise monopolar coagulation was performed directly on the bleeding arterial branch, starting from the base of the vessel to ensure complete vascular sealing, followed by coagulation of the pseudoaneurysm wall to prevent recurrent hemorrhage. The procedure was conducted carefully to maintain optimal endoscopic visibility and avoid excessive thermal injury to the surrounding renal parenchyma. The coagulations were performed using a Karl Storz monopolar TURB resectoscope system (Karl Storz SE & Co. KG, Tuttlingen, Germany). Upon completion, the treated area was thoroughly inspected, confirming complete hemostasis with no residual active bleeding or vascular oozing. Antegrade DJ stent 4.8 F was inserted. Following successful hemostasis, a 16F Foley catheter was used as a temporary nephrostomy and tamponade device (Fig. 2). The catheter was introduced through the established percutaneous nephrostomy tract into the target calyx within the collecting system. A small amount of contrast was injected under fluoroscopic guidance to confirm accurate intrarenal positioning of the catheter tip and balloon. Subsequently, the balloon was inflated with 3 mL of water and positioned to achieve local tamponade adjacent to the lesion, while ensuring adequate drainage. The patient's postoperative course was uneventful, and the balloon nephrostomy tube was removed two days after the procedure. The patient was subsequently discharged with stable vital signs and no further episodes of hematuria. DJ stent was removed under local anesthesia two weeks later.

A 36-year-old multiparous woman, with a body mass index of 27.7 kg/m2, one prior caesarian section in 2019 and no significant comorbidities, presented with a severe RD, measuring 15 cm at rest and expanding to 25 cm during the Valsalva maneuver, associated with an umbilical hernia, both confirmed by a computed tomography (CT). These findings were accompanied by significant abdominal skin excess following three pregnancies and postpartum weight fluctuations (Fig. 1). She reported core weakness, lower back pain, and severe body image dissatisfaction. The patient received intravenous prophylactic Cefuroxim prior to skin incision. A standard abdominoplasty approach was performed. A 30 × 15 cm abdominal dermal flap was harvested, deepithelialized, resected, and defatted using a sharp facelift scissor to remove the subcutaneous adipose tissue, with care to preserve a uniform dermal thickness. Methylene blue dye was used intraoperatively to ensure complete deepithelialization and guide final graft shaping (Fig. 2). The autologous dermal graft was then positioned in the retro-rectus space (sublay) according to the Rives–Stoppa technique and fixed with interrupted Vycril 2.0 stitches (Ethicon Inc., USA) to the posterior rectus sheath. The anterior rectus fascia was then closed by two overlaps of Maxon 2.0 running sutures (Ethicon Inc., USA) (Fig. 3). After repositioning the abdominal flap, the superficial fascial layer was closed with Vicryl 2.0 (Ethicon Inc., USA). Two subcutaneous drains and one retromuscular drain were placed and secured. The incision was then closed with reversed Monocryl 3.0 suture and completed with a Monocryl 4.0 running intradermal suture (Ethicon Inc, USA). The umbilicus was then repositioned and umbilicoplasty was performed using an inverted-U incision and secured in place using reversed intradermal Monocryl 3.0 suture and Prolene 5.0 Allgöwer-Donati sutures (Ethicon Inc, USA) (Fig. 3). An abdominal compressive garment was applied at the end of the procedure. One week postoperatively, the patient required surgical debridement for umbilical necrosis followed by immediate reconstruction using local flaps. The postoperative course thereafter was uncomplicated. The patient declined further umbilical scar revision. At the one-year follow-up, clinical examination and ultrasound imaging showed no recurrence of RD, and the patient expressed high satisfaction with both functional improvement and cosmetic outcome (Fig. 4).

An 89-year-old woman (G5P5), menopausal since age 48, presented with one month of heavy vaginal bleeding, saturating approximately 10 pads per day. Associated symptoms included lightheadedness, fatigue, pelvic pain, nausea, and decreased appetite. Family history was notable for gastric cancer in her mother and breast cancer in her sister. Pelvic examination revealed a smooth but markedly enlarged and firm cervix with dark blood at the external os. Differential considerations included cervical carcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, and lymphoma. Examination under anesthesia with cervical biopsies and loop electrosurgical excision procedure was performed. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 10.1 × 10.5 × 10.2 cm mass involving the entire cervix, with possible extension into the lower uterine segment. The endometrial canal, containing air from a recent biopsy, was displaced anteriorly by posterior myometrial invasion measuring 5.2 × 3.6 × 4.1 cm (Fig. 1). A mildly enlarged left external iliac lymph node measuring 1.1 × 1.3 cm was present (Fig. 2). No ascites or peritoneal masses were identified. The ovaries appeared normal. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated diffuse enlargement of the cervix with loss of the normal three-zone cervical anatomy. A large mass replaced the entire cervix, extended into the posterior uterine body, and appeared mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted (T2W) imaging. The normal inner low–T2 stromal ring and outer intermediate–T2 stroma were completely replaced by abnormal, heterogeneous high T2 signal. The endocervical canal demonstrated preserved high T2 signal, and the ectocervical contour remained smooth despite marked cervical expansion. The infiltrative mass in the posterior body of the uterus displaced the endometrium anteriorly (Fig. 3). Following administration of 8 mL of intravenous gadobutrol (Gadavist; Bayer, Leverkusen, Germany), T1-weighted (T1W) fat-saturated images demonstrated diffuse, heterogeneous enhancement of the cervical mass, while the endocervical canal remained preserved and hypointense (Fig. No cystic change or tumor necrosis was identified. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) demonstrated marked diffusion restriction, with the cervical mass appearing hyperintense on DWI and correspondingly hypointense on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map (Fig. 5A, B), consistent with high tumor cellularity. FDG-PET/CT revealed intense hypermetabolism of the cervical mass, with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 35.2, extending into the uterus (Fig. 6A). A left external iliac lymph node measuring 1.2 cm demonstrated marked hypermetabolism SUVmax of 25.2 (Fig. Additional mildly hypermetabolic mediastinal and left supraclavicular lymph nodes were present, with SUVmax values ranging from 2.5 to 3.9 (Fig. The spleen was normal, and no osseous lesions were identified. Histologic examination demonstrated diffuse effacement of the cervical stroma by sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells, consistent with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) according to the World Health Organization Classification of Tumours of Haematolymphoid Neoplasms, 5th edition (2022). The neoplastic cells exhibited vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, frequent mitotic figures, and numerous apoptotic bodies. Scattered tingible body macrophages were present, producing a characteristic starry-sky appearance (Fig. Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse positivity for CD20 and expression of CD10, consistent with a germinal center B-cell subtype. BCL2 was positive, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 95%, indicating a high proliferative rate.

A 64-year-old postmenopausal woman under hormonal substitution with a history of surgically treated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia 3 (VIN 3) and a positive family history of gynecological cancers was referred to our institution for further evaluation following a positive breast cancer screening. Bilateral screening mammography revealed a 1-cm spiculated mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, in proximity to pleomorphic segmentary micro- and macrocalcifications (Fig. 1A,C), classified as BI-RADS 5 (highly suggestive of malignancy, >95%). In the contralateral breast, an irregular 1-cm mass with fine clustered microcalcifications was detected in the lower inner quadrant (Fig. 1B,D), classified as BI-RADS 4C (high suspicion for malignancy, 50%-94%). Targeted US of the right breast confirmed a heterogeneous hypoechoic lesion in the upper outer quadrant, with an echogenic rim and internal color Doppler vascularity, measuring approximately 1 × 0.7 × 0.7 cm and located 4 cm from the nipple (Fig. An US-guided core biopsy of the lesion using an 18-gauge Biopince BioPinceTM automated core biopsy instrument (Argon Medical Devices, INC) was performed in the same session without immediate complications. Histopathological analysis confirmed an invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST), grade 3, triple negative (ER-, PR-, HER2-), with a high proliferative index (Ki-67 80%) and choriocarcinomatous differentiation. To evaluate the adjacent pleomorphic segmentary micro- and macrocalcifications, which were not visible on US, a tomosynthesis-guided VABB was subsequently performed: We used a Hologic Affirm table with the patient in prone position and standard mediolateral compression of the right breast. An initially obtained localizing tomosynthesis acquisition of the right breast allowed target selection of the most suspicious area of the microcalcifications. Local anesthesia of the skin and biopsy trajectory was administered. A 9-gauge Eviva needle (Guided Breast Biopsy Device, Hologic, Inc.) was inserted approximately 7 cm deep using a cranial approach. The needle aperture of 20 mm was positioned exactly in front of the target. A vacuum assisted sample aspiration, yielding 12 tissue samples, without immediate adverse events was performed. Post-biopsy tomosynthesis confirmed adequate retrieval of the calcifications (Fig. Subsequently a biopsy clip was inserted. Standard post-biopsy manual breast compression was applied for approximately 10 minutes with the patient in the supine position following a compressive dressing with an elastic bandage. The patient underwent clinical evaluation 1 hour after the procedure and was discharged home after an unremarkable examination. Three days later, a staging breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed the well-known spiculated lesion in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast corresponding to the biopsy-proven invasive carcinoma (Fig. 4A). The BI-RADS 4C lesion of the lower inner quadrant of the left breast presented a non-mass enhancement, defined as enhancement without a corresponding discrete mass or space-occupying lesion (Fig. 4B). Incidentally, at the site of the VABB in the upper quadrants of the right breast, a large multiloculated intramammary hematoma of approximately 10×7×7.5 cm was observed, responsible for breast swelling and associated with hematoma-related skin edema and infiltration (Fig. Within the hematoma, a well-circumscribed oval lesion measuring 1.4 cm x 1.1 cm in diameter in the axial plane, of mixed signal on T1 and T2, showing avid and early enhancement was identified in the upper inner quadrant, 8.5 cm from the nipple, consistent with the circulating lumen of a PSA, supplied by a feeding artery arising from the internal mammary artery. Retrospectively, the patient reported progressive right breast swelling and discomfort since the biopsy procedure. Given these findings, the patient was referred to our interventional radiology department for targeted color Doppler US evaluation 5 days later. This confirmed a PSA in the right breast, with a patent circulating lumen of 0.7 cm showing marked turbulent flow and a partially thrombosed sac measuring 2.6 cm (Fig. A classic “yin-yang” sign and/or “to-and-fro” waveform were not explicitly documented. The discrepancy in measurements between MRI and ultrasound likely reflects the dynamic character of these lesions, with the MRI demonstrating a larger circulating lumen and the ultrasound performed 5 days later showing reduction of the residual lumen, consistent with progressive thrombosis. Furthermore, differences in patient positioning between MRI and ultrasound examinations may also have contributed, to a lesser extent, to the variation in pseudoaneurysm measurements. A decision was made to treat the PSA with percutaneous thrombin injection. Under strict aseptic conditions, sterile draping and local anesthesia (Lidocaine 1%, 10ml) a 19-gauge spinal needle was advanced under US-guidance into the PSA lumen, followed by slow injection of 2 ml of fibrin sealant (TisseelⓇ, Baxter AG).

A male neonate, aged 1 day, born at term following an uneventful pregnancy, was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for acute respiratory distress. The patient was born to first-degree consanguineous parents. The mother was aged 34 years, gravida 3 para 3, with no significant obstetrical history. Prenatal follow-up was regular, and no fetal abnormalities were detected on antenatal ultrasonography. Birth weight was 3200 g, 49 cm, and Apgar scores were 5 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. On admission, the newborn was tonic and reactive. Respiratory examination revealed marked tachypnea with an oxygen saturation of 79% on room air, associated with severe signs of respiratory distress, including pronounced intercostal and subcostal retractions, nasal flaring, and a narrow, constricted thoracic cage (Fig. 1). Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Due to worsening respiratory failure, the patient was transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit and required endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Postintubation oxygen saturation improved to 93% under ventilatory support. Despite initial stabilization, lung compliance remained poor, consistent with a restrictive ventilatory pattern related to chest wall abnormality. A chest radiograph obtained at admission demonstrated a short, narrow, elongated thoracic cage with reduced transverse diameter, high-riding clavicles with a characteristic “handlebar” appearance, and irregular costochondral junctions, raising suspicion for an underlying skeletal dysplasia (Fig. 2). Thoracic computed tomography performed to identify the cause of respiratory distress confirmed the severe thoracic narrowing with short, horizontally oriented ribs and elevated clavicles. Additionally, bilateral pulmonary consolidations consistent with infectious pneumonia were observed (Fig. 3). Supplementary Videos 1 and 2 provide axial CT images and 3D volume-rendered reconstructions of the thoracic skeletal abnormalities. Pelvic radiography revealed dysplastic acetabula with flattened acetabular roofs, trident-shaped acetabula, short and flared iliac bones, and shortened femora (Fig. 4). Radiographs of the extremities additionally demonstrated shortening of the long bones associated with metaphyseal irregularities (Fig. 5). The combination of thoracic and pelvic skeletal abnormalities was highly suggestive of a ciliopathy-related skeletal dysplasia, most consistent with asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (Jeune syndrome). The patient remained hospitalized in the neonatal intensive care unit for 7 days, requiring continuous invasive mechanical ventilation and receiving broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy for bilateral infectious pneumonia. Despite intensive supportive care, the respiratory condition progressively worsened due to severe thoracic restriction complicated by pulmonary infection. The neonate ultimately developed refractory respiratory failure and died during the hospital stay. No autopsy was performed.

A 49-year-old male presented to the accident and emergency department of Santa Teresa Hospital with an acute infection and severe pain localized in the right mandibular region. The patient reported a 4-week history of persistent symptoms following tooth extraction, with a nonhealing postextraction socket and continuous purulent discharge. Initial management prior to hospital admission included oral antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin–clavulanate (Clavulin BD 875 mg, every 12 hours for 14 days), without clinical improvement. The patient’s medical history was significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus and active smoking habit. He denied any previous surgical history and reported no relevant family history of systemic diseases. Clinical examination revealed pronounced trismus, local oedema, tenderness on palpation, and active purulent exudate from the affected alveolus. Laboratory tests demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers, with a leukocyte count of 11,300 cells/µL (reference range: 4000-10,000 cells/µL) and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 8.9 mg/dL (reference value: <0.5 mg/dL), consistent with an active infectious process and significantly higher than normal values reported in the literature. Computed tomography (CT) of the postextraction alveolar region of tooth no. 47 revealed irregular and poorly defined areas of bone sclerosis, disruption of the cortical plates, particularly at the lingual mandibular cortical margin, and evidence of pathological fracture in this region (Fig. 1). Additionally, bone sequestra were identified as isolated radiopaque fragments within a radiolucent area, consistent with avascular necrotic bone. Given the severity of the condition, surgical treatment consisting of en bloc mandibular resection with adequate safety margins was initially proposed. However, the patient declined this approach and opted for a less invasive treatment strategy. A conservative surgical approach was therefore performed under local anesthesia, consisting of curettage of the affected alveolar region using a spherical bur, removal of bone sequestra, debridement of adjacent infected tissues, and copious irrigation with sterile saline solution prior to the initiation of antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT). Subsequently, aPDT was performed using 0.01% methylene blue activated by a 660 nm low-level laser, followed by adjunctive low-level infrared laser therapy for photobiomodulation. Multiple treatment sessions were carried out, with monthly radiographic follow-up over a 6-month outpatient period. After irrigating the surgical cavity with sterile saline solution and gently drying it, a 0.01% MB solution was applied to the affected area using a blunt cannula, with a total volume of approximately 0.5 mL. A preirradiation time of 5 minutes was used to allow adequate penetration of the photosensitiser. The irradiation was performed using a low-intensity red laser (660 nm, continuous wave, 100 mW). The energy applied ranged from 6 J per spot, with an exposure time of 60 seconds per spot, covering the entire affected area and its margins. The sessions were carried out once a week for 4 weeks. Infrared laser therapy (808 nm, 100 mW) was applied in contact mode to the mandibular region to promote tissue repair and modulate inflammation. Energy doses of 8 J per point were administered at 8 points spaced approximately 1 cm apart. Sessions were conducted twice a week for 4 weeks, totaling 8 sessions on alternate days with the application of red laser. Patients were clinically re-evaluated during each session. A progressive reduction in pain was observed during the first 2 weeks of treatment. After the second aPDT session, purulent drainage resolved completely, accompanied by a significant reduction in oedema and bone tenderness. No clinical signs of infection progression were detected during follow-up. Radiographic assessment was performed using panoramic radiographs at monthly intervals following the start of the treatment protocol, over a period of 6 months. Imaging studies demonstrated a progressive reduction in intraosseous radiolucent areas, associated with peripheral bone formation in previously affected regions (Fig. 2, Fig. 3).
